President Bola Tinubu has forwarded the National Mental Health Amendment Bill 2026 to the Senate, seeking to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide and provide care and support for survivors. The letter conveying the proposed legislation was read by the President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, during plenary on Tuesday. In the letter, Tinubu said the bill sought to amend the National Mental Health Act 2021 by decriminalising attempted suicide and ensuring that people who survive such attempts receive appropriate support. “Pursuant to Section 58, subsection 2 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, as amended, I forward herewith the National Mental Health Amendment Bill 2026 for the kind consideration of the Nigerian Senate,” the President said. He expressed hope that the lawmakers would give the bill expeditious consideration. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources The President’s move comes amid a legislative debate over the criminalisation of attempted suicide, following the Senate’s passage of a separate bill on the matter for second reading. The bill, sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who represents Cross River South, seeks to replace criminal punishment with medical treatment, rehabilitation and other support measures. Leading the debate, Ekpenyong argued that Nigeria’s legal framework was inconsistent, noting that while the National Mental Health Act recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate intervention, the Criminal Code and Penal Code still treat it as an offence. He warned that criminalising attempted suicide could discourage people experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help and make families conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma. Ekpenyong said the proposal raised a fundamental question about whether the state should respond to people who survive suicide attempts with prosecution or protection. During the earlier debate, Akpabio had opposed the proposed decriminalisation, insisting that people who attempted suicide should face imprisonment if they survived. “As far as we are concerned, we are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, you better succeed. If you don’t succeed, we will send you to prison,” the Senate President had said. However, reacting to Tinubu’s letter on Tuesday, Akpabio welcomed the proposed amendment, clarifying that his earlier position did not include people experiencing mental health challenges. “I did not include people who are mentally disturbed because they don’t have a mental balance to know what they are doing,” he said. He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health challenges would be insensitive, maintaining that his earlier comments had distinguished between those who were mentally sound and those who were mentally disturbed. Akpabio subsequently referred the amendment bill to the Senate Committee on Rules and Business for further legislative action.
